expectedText:
APPORTIONMENT OF A SEPARATE-PROPERTY BUSINESS GROWN BY COMMUNITY EFFORT (PEREIRA/VAN CAMP) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

PURPOSE AND IDENTIFICATION OF THE SEPARATE-PROPERTY BUSINESS
This document concerns Lee Precision Machining, Inc., a business in which Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee holds, or claims to hold, a separate property interest, in connection with the dissolution of their marriage. The parties married on June 14, 2015 and separated on March 2, 2026. It states legal background on how California courts have apportioned, between the community and the owning spouse's separate estate, the increase in value or profits of a separate-property business to which a spouse devoted personal effort during the marriage -- the approaches commonly called the Pereira and Van Camp formulas -- and the general community and separate property statutes from which that case law proceeds. This document is not a court order, is not a valuation of Lee Precision Machining, Inc., and does not state whether any part of the value or profits of Lee Precision Machining, Inc. is community property, separate property, or a combination of both.

GENERAL RULE: PROPERTY ACQUIRED DURING MARRIAGE IS COMMUNITY PROPERTY
As a general rule, property acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in California is community property, except as otherwise provided by statute. This baseline rule is one of the two statutory starting points for the apportionment question addressed by this document, because the earnings a spouse produces through personal skill, effort, and labor during the marriage fall within it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Except as otherwise provided by statute, all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is community property."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 760 (California Legislative Information text), the general definition of community property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=760.)
  Known gap: This is a single, general statutory rule (Cal. Fam. Code § 760) subject to numerous statutory exceptions that are outside the scope of this clause. It does not by itself resolve how the profits or growth of a business owned as separate property, but worked on by a spouse during the marriage, are characterized; that question is addressed by the case-law clauses elsewhere in this document.

STATUTORY RULE: PROPERTY OWNED BEFORE MARRIAGE, AND ITS RENTS, ISSUES, AND PROFITS, ARE SEPARATE PROPERTY
The Family Code provides that the separate property of a married person includes all property the person owned before marriage, all property acquired after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent, and the "rents, issues, and profits" of that property. A business owned before marriage is therefore separate property, and so, in general, is income the business produces on account of its own capital and character. Read together with the community property rule in the preceding clause, this provision creates the apportionment question the courts have addressed: when a separate-property business grows or produces profit during marriage partly because of its own capital and partly because of the owning spouse's personal effort (which is a community asset), some allocation between the two estates is required.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "(a) Separate property of a married person includes all of the following: (1) All property owned by the person before marriage. (2) All property acquired by the person after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent. (3) The rents, issues, and profits of the property described in this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 770(a) (California Legislative Information text), definition of separate property, including rents, issues, and profits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=770.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivision (a) of Cal. Fam. Code § 770; subdivision (b), which concerns a married person's power to convey separate property without the spouse's consent, is omitted as not relevant here. The statute itself contains no apportionment formula and does not mention the Pereira or Van Camp approaches; those are judicial constructs described in the following clauses. At the time the earliest decisions cited in this document were issued, the predecessor of this provision was codified at former Civil Code section 163 (later section 5108); the current codification is quoted here.

CASE LAW: THE PEREIRA APPROACH -- A FAIR RETURN TO SEPARATE CAPITAL, THE EXCESS TO THE COMMUNITY
In Pereira v. Pereira (1909), the California Supreme Court reviewed a divorce judgment that had treated all of a husband's business gains after marriage as community property, without any allowance for the $15,500 of separate capital he had invested in the business before marriage. The Court held this was error. It reasoned that the capital was the husband's separate estate; that although the principal part of the large income was clearly due to the husband's personal character, energy, ability, and capacity (a share that was "of course" community property), the business could not have been carried on without the capital; and that, absent circumstances showing a different result, some of the profits are presumed justly due to the capital invested. The Court directed that the probable contribution of the capital be determined from all the circumstances, and that for a profitable business it would amount at least to the usual interest on a long, well-secured investment. The apportionment method that developed from this decision -- allocating a fair return on the separate capital to the separate estate and the excess of the profits or growth to the community -- is commonly called the Pereira approach.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "This capital was undoubtedly his separate estate. The fund remained in the business after marriage and was used by him in carrying it on. The separate property should have been credited with some amount as profit on this capital. It was not a losing business but a very profitable one. It is true that it is very clearly shown that the principal part of the large income was due to the personal character, energy, ability, and capacity of the husband. This share of the earnings was, of course, community property. But without capital he could not have carried on the business."
  — Pereira v. Pereira (1909) 156 Cal. 1, 156 Cal. 1, 7 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3303139/pereira-v-pereira/)
  "The probable contribution of the capital to the income should have been determined from all the circumstances of the case, and as the business was profitable it would amount at least to the usual interest on a long investment well secured."
  — Pereira v. Pereira (1909) 156 Cal. 1, 156 Cal. 1, 7 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3303139/pereira-v-pereira/)
  Known gap: This is a 1909 California Supreme Court decision applying former Civil Code section 163 and the divorce statutes of that era; it predates the Family Code, no-fault dissolution, and the equal-division rule. The Court did not state a specific percentage as the fair return; it described only a floor ("at least" the usual interest on a long, well-secured investment) and left the amount to be determined on remand from all the circumstances. The decision does not use the label "Pereira approach"; that label was attached by later courts, as described in the Beam clause of this document. The Court also reversed the community property finding for retrial rather than fixing the apportionment itself.

CASE LAW: THE VAN CAMP APPROACH -- REASONABLE VALUE OF THE SPOUSE'S SERVICES TO THE COMMUNITY, THE BALANCE TO SEPARATE CAPITAL
In Van Camp v. Van Camp (1921), the Court of Appeal considered a husband who owned, before marriage, most of the stock of a sea food packing corporation he had organized, who devoted his exclusive time and effort to managing it during the marriage, and who was paid a salary by the corporation for doing so. The wife argued, relying on Pereira, that the community should receive all profits above a seven percent return on the capital. The court found the Pereira circumstances inapplicable on those facts. It reasoned that, although the corporation's success was to a large extent due to the husband's capacity and ability, the business could not have been conducted without the invested capital, and the husband had been paid what the evidence showed was an adequate salary for services that another person of equal capacity could have been hired to perform. The court concluded that the husband's compensation must be deemed the extent of his personal earnings (community property), and that the balance of the business's profits was attributable to the capital invested (separate property), just as if he had not been employed by the corporation. The resulting method -- valuing the community's services, allocating that amount to the community, and treating the remainder as separate property -- is commonly called the Van Camp approach.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "While it may be true that the success of the corporation of which defendant was president and manager was to a large extent due to his capacity and ability, nevertheless without the investment of his and other capital in the corporation he could not have conducted the business, and while he devoted his energies and personal efforts to making it a success, he was by the corporation paid what the evidence shows was an adequate salary, and for which another than himself with equal capacity could have been secured."
  — Van Camp v. Van Camp (1921) 53 Cal.App. 17, 53 Cal.App. 17, 28 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3287636/van-camp-v-van-camp/)
  "must be deemed the extent of his personal earnings, and the balance of the profits derived from the business accredited to the use of the capital invested therein, in the same manner as though he had not been employed by the corporation."
  — Van Camp v. Van Camp (1921) 53 Cal.App. 17, 53 Cal.App. 17, 29 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3287636/van-camp-v-van-camp/)
  Known gap: This is a 1921 Court of Appeal decision (review denied by the California Supreme Court on July 25, 1921), decided under former Civil Code section 163 and the fault-based divorce statutes of that era. The decision also addressed grounds for divorce, the family-expense presumption, and the sufficiency of the evidence on the value of the community estate, none of which is described here. The court's conclusion rested in part on its findings that the corporation was a genuine entity separate from the husband and that his salary was adequate; it did not announce a general rule that a salaried spouse's business profits are always separate property. The opinion, as stored on CourtListener, is an OCR scan and contains scattered stray characters (for example, a small square symbol and a stray accent) in passages not quoted here; the quoted passages were confirmed free of such artifacts.

WHEN APPORTIONMENT IS REQUIRED: MORE THAN MINIMAL COMMUNITY EFFORT DEVOTED TO SEPARATE PROPERTY
The California Supreme Court in Beam v. Bank of America (1971) restated the principle underlying both approaches: because income arising from a spouse's skill, efforts, and industry is community property, the community is entitled to a fair share of the profits that derive from the spouse's devotion of more than minimal time and effort to handling his or her separate property. The Court of Appeal in In re Marriage of Dekker (1993) read Pereira the same way, stating that where more than minimal community effort combines with a separate capital investment to increase the value of the separate investment, the court must determine the amount of the increase attributable to the capital and the amount attributable to community effort. In In re Marriage of Brooks (2019), the Court of Appeal observed that the decision to apportion at all presupposes that the spouse made more than minimal contributions to the separate-property business during the marriage; if the contributions were minimal, no apportionment method would need to be chosen because there would be no potential community interest. Under these decisions, the threshold question is whether the spouse's efforts during marriage exceeded a minimal level; only then does the choice between the Pereira and Van Camp approaches arise.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Nevertheless, long ago our courts recognized that, since income arising from the husband's skill, efforts and industry is community property, the community should receive a fair share of the profits which derive from the husband's devotion of more than minimal time and effort to the handling of his separate property."
  — Beam v. Bank of America (1971) 6 Cal.3d 12, 6 Cal.3d 12, 17 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1436884/beam-v-bank-of-america/)
  "A fair reading of Pereira supports the view that where more than minimal community effort combines with a separate capital investment to increase the value of the separate investment, the court must determine the amount of the increase attributable to the capital, and the amount attributable to community effort."
  — In re Marriage of Dekker (1993) 17 Cal.App.4th 842, 17 Cal.App.4th 842, 852 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256848/in-re-marriage-of-dekker/)
  "In fact, the decision to apportion presupposes that Husband made more than minimal contributions to the separate property business during the marriage."
  — In re Marriage of Brooks (2019) 33 Cal.App.5th 576, 33 Cal.App.5th 576 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/6107290/brooks-v-brooks-in-re-brooks/)
  Known gap: The decisions quoted here describe the threshold in qualitative terms ("more than minimal") and do not define it numerically or by hours worked. Beam involved a husband's management of an inherited investment estate rather than an operating business, and the Court there ultimately concluded that no net community property existed under either approach on the facts before it. Brooks's statement was made in the course of affirming a Van Camp allocation on a substantial-evidence standard of review; it is a Court of Appeal decision and not a California Supreme Court holding. This clause does not describe how the community's resulting share, once determined, is divided between the spouses.

CASE LAW: BEAM'S DESCRIPTION OF THE TWO ALTERNATIVE APPORTIONMENT APPROACHES
In Beam v. Bank of America (1971), the California Supreme Court described the two "quite distinct, alternative approaches" California courts had evolved for allocating earnings between separate and community income when a spouse devotes effort to separate property. The Pereira approach, the Court explained, is to allocate a fair return on the separate property investment as separate income and to allocate any excess to the community as arising from the spouse's efforts. The Van Camp approach is to determine the reasonable value of the spouse's services, allocate that amount as community property, and treat the balance as separate property attributable to the normal earnings of the separate estate. The two methods therefore start from opposite ends: Pereira fixes the separate estate's share first (a return on capital) and gives the community the remainder, while Van Camp fixes the community's share first (the value of the services) and gives the separate estate the remainder.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "is to allocate a fair return on the [husband's separate property] investment [as separate income] and to allocate any excess to the community property as arising from the husband's efforts."
  — Beam v. Bank of America (1971) 6 Cal.3d 12, 6 Cal.3d 12, 18 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1436884/beam-v-bank-of-america/)
  "to determine the reasonable value of the husband's services . . . , allocate that amount as community property, and treat the balance as separate property attributable to the normal earnings of the [separate estate]."
  — Beam v. Bank of America (1971) 6 Cal.3d 12, 6 Cal.3d 12, 18 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1436884/beam-v-bank-of-america/)
  Known gap: Beam quoted these descriptions from earlier decisions (Estate of Neilson (1962) 57 Cal.2d 733 and Tassi v. Tassi (1958) 160 Cal.App.2d 680) rather than formulating them anew; the bracketed words in the quotations are the Beam Court's own insertions. Beam involved separate property consisting of an inherited estate managed by the husband, not an operating business he founded; the Court applied the same apportionment principles to both situations. The Court used the gendered terms of the era ("husband's"); the principles apply to either spouse.

CASE LAW: NO FIXED STANDARD FOR CHOOSING BETWEEN THE APPROACHES; THE COURT SELECTS THE FORMULA THAT ACHIEVES SUBSTANTIAL JUSTICE
Beam also stated the governing principle for choosing between the two approaches. Quoting earlier Court of Appeal authority, the California Supreme Court explained that California courts have developed no precise criterion or fixed standard for making the apportionment, but have endeavored to adopt the yardstick that is most appropriate and equitable in the particular situation, depending on whether the character of the capital investment in the separate property or the personal activity, ability, and capacity of the spouse is the chief contributing factor in producing the income and profits. In applying this principle, the trial court is not bound either to adopt a predetermined percentage as a fair return on separate business capital (the Pereira approach) nor to limit the community interest to a salary fixed as the reward for a spouse's services (the Van Camp method), but may select whichever formula will achieve substantial justice between the parties. Later decisions, including Dekker (1993), Brandes (2015), and Brooks (2019), have repeated this formulation as the controlling standard.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "In making such apportionment between separate and community property our courts have developed no precise criterion or fixed standard, but have endeavored to adopt that yardstick which is most appropriate and equitable in a particular situation . . . depending on whether the character of the capital investment in the separate property or the personal activity, ability, and capacity of the spouse is the chief contributing factor in the realization of income and profits"
  — Beam v. Bank of America (1971) 6 Cal.3d 12, 6 Cal.3d 12, 18 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1436884/beam-v-bank-of-america/)
  "In applying this principle of apportionment the court is not bound either to adopt a predetermined percentage as a fair return on business capital which is separate property [the Pereira approach] nor need it limit the community interest only to [a] salary fixed as the reward for a spouse's service [the Van Camp method] but may select [whichever] formula will achieve substantial justice between the parties."
  — Beam v. Bank of America (1971) 6 Cal.3d 12, 6 Cal.3d 12, 18 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1436884/beam-v-bank-of-america/)
  Known gap: The quoted language is Beam's quotation of Logan v. Forster (1952) 114 Cal.App.2d 587, 599-600; the bracketed labels "[the Pereira approach]" and "[the Van Camp method]" were inserted by the Beam Court. The "chief contributing factor" test is stated as a guide to the trial court's discretion, not as a mechanical rule, and Beam itself declined to decide whether the trial court there had erred in choosing Pereira because the result was the same under Van Camp. This clause does not address other apportionment methods that have occasionally been used (for example, the so-called Todd formula noted in a Dekker footnote), which Beam does not discuss.

CASE LAW: THE LEGAL INTEREST RATE AS THE PEREIRA "REASONABLE RATE OF RETURN" ABSENT OTHER EVIDENCE
Beam also addressed what rate of return on separate capital a court may use under the Pereira approach. The trial court there had adopted the legal interest rate of seven percent simple interest as the reasonable rate of return on the husband's separate property. The wife argued on appeal that this figure was unrealistically high, but she had introduced no evidence at trial supporting any other, more realistic rate. The California Supreme Court, citing its earlier decision in Weinberg v. Weinberg (1967), stated that in the absence of such evidence the trial court correctly adopted the rate of legal interest. Under Beam, therefore, the legal interest rate serves as a default measure of the separate estate's fair return under Pereira when neither party presents evidence of a different rate, while leaving the parties free to prove that a different rate is appropriate in their case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "In applying the Pereira formula the trial court adopted the legal interest rate of 7 percent simple interest as the "reasonable rate of return" on Mr. Beam's separate property; although the wife now attacks this 7 percent simple interest figure as unrealistically high, at trial she introduced no evidence in support of any other more "realistic" rate of return"
  — Beam v. Bank of America (1971) 6 Cal.3d 12, 6 Cal.3d 12, 19 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1436884/beam-v-bank-of-america/)
  "in the absence of such evidence "the trial court correctly adopted the rate of legal interest.""
  — Beam v. Bank of America (1971) 6 Cal.3d 12, 6 Cal.3d 12, 19 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1436884/beam-v-bank-of-america/)
  Known gap: The seven percent figure reflects the legal interest rate in effect at the time of the Beam trial; Beam does not hold that seven percent is the fair return in every case, and Dekker (1993), described elsewhere in this document, affirmed a trial court's use of a ten percent annual return on the facts of that case. This clause does not state the current legal or judgment interest rate in California, which is set by separate constitutional and statutory provisions not cited here. The two quotations come from a single sentence in Beam, split around a citation to Weinberg; the second quotation is Beam's own quotation of Weinberg.

CASE LAW: COMMUNITY LIVING EXPENSES ARE DEDUCTED FROM APPORTIONED COMMUNITY INCOME
Beam further explained a step that follows the apportionment under either approach. Once a court ascertains the amount of community income through the Pereira or Van Camp method, it deducts the community's living expenses from that community income to determine the balance of community property, applying the presumption that family living expenses are paid from community earnings rather than from separate funds. The Court described this "family expense presumption" as one that prior California decisions applying either formula had universally invoked. In Beam itself, the parties' living expenses of about $24,000 per year exceeded the community income of $17,000 per year that the Van Camp approach would have yielded, so the Court concluded that no positive balance of community property had ever accumulated from the husband's management of his separate estate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "it deducts the community's living expenses from community income to determine the balance of the community property."
  — Beam v. Bank of America (1971) 6 Cal.3d 12, 6 Cal.3d 12, 21 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1436884/beam-v-bank-of-america/)
  "This "family expense presumption" has been universally invoked by prior California decisions applying either the Pereira or Van Camp formula."
  — Beam v. Bank of America (1971) 6 Cal.3d 12, 6 Cal.3d 12, 21 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1436884/beam-v-bank-of-america/)
  Known gap: This clause describes the family-expense presumption only as Beam applied it to income apportioned from a spouse's separate property; it does not address the presumption's operation in other contexts, such as tracing separate funds through a commingled account, or the effect of a spouse's testimony about which funds were actually used to pay expenses (an argument the Beam Court considered and rejected on its facts). Beam involved income from a managed investment estate; whether and how the presumption operates when the apportioned community interest is in the retained growth in value of an operating business, rather than in distributed income, is not addressed by the quoted passages. The first quotation in this clause omits the beginning of the source sentence, which in the CourtListener text contains a doubled comma typographical artifact ("approach,, it deducts"); the quotation begins after that artifact rather than reproducing or silently correcting it.

CASE LAW: DEKKER'S STATEMENT OF WHEN EACH APPROACH IS TYPICALLY APPLIED
In In re Marriage of Dekker (1993), the Court of Appeal summarized the circumstances in which each approach is typically used. Pereira is typically applied where the business profits are principally attributed to the efforts of the community. Conversely, Van Camp is applied where community effort is more than minimally involved in a separate business, yet the profits are attributed to the character of the separate asset itself. The court affirmed a trial court's application of Pereira to a corporation whose stock had been issued to the wife as her separate property but which the husband, devoting all of his time and effort, had built from an initial $1,000 investment into a business valued at $927,000 at trial; the trial court allocated the wife's original $1,000 plus a ten percent annual return to her separate property and the balance (about $925,000) to the community.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Pereira is typically applied where business profits are principally attributed to efforts of the community."
  — In re Marriage of Dekker (1993) 17 Cal.App.4th 842, 17 Cal.App.4th 842, 853 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256848/in-re-marriage-of-dekker/)
  "Conversely, Van Camp is applied where community effort is more than minimally involved in a separate business, yet the business profits accrued are attributed to the character of the separate asset."
  — In re Marriage of Dekker (1993) 17 Cal.App.4th 842, 17 Cal.App.4th 842, 853 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256848/in-re-marriage-of-dekker/)
  Known gap: This is a single published Court of Appeal decision (Fourth Appellate District, Division One). Its characterizations of when each approach is "typically" applied are descriptive summaries of prior case law, not mandatory rules, and Dekker itself reiterated that the trial court has discretion to choose whichever formula will effect substantial justice. Dekker involved an unusual fact pattern in which the separate property belonged to the non-working spouse; the court held that Pereira applies regardless of which spouse owns the separate capital. The figures in this clause are drawn from the opinion's recitation of the trial court's findings and are stated as facts of that case only.

CASE LAW: PAYMENT OF A MARKET SALARY TO THE WORKING SPOUSE DOES NOT BY ITSELF END THE INQUIRY
Dekker rejected the argument that no apportionment was needed because the working spouse had already been paid market-value compensation for his services during the marriage. The Court of Appeal held that whether or not the community received a salary, a court must determine to what extent the increased value of the separate-property business is attributable to community effort. On the facts of that case, the court reasoned that limiting the community to the compensation it received by way of salary would ignore California's egalitarian marriage model and the Pereira apportionment formula, and would leave more than $925,000 of increase in value unattributed to either estate. It also rejected the characterization of the result as a "double dip" for the working spouse, observing that the salary was itself community property in which both spouses had shared, but that the salary did not fairly reflect the community's efforts that had built the business.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Whether or not the community received salary, a court must determine to what extent the increased value of the separate property business is attributable to community effort."
  — In re Marriage of Dekker (1993) 17 Cal.App.4th 842, 17 Cal.App.4th 842, 852 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256848/in-re-marriage-of-dekker/)
  "To limit the community to compensation received by way of salary during the marriage would ignore California's egalitarian marriage model and the apportionment formula of Pereira, and thereby leave over $925,000 unattributed."
  — In re Marriage of Dekker (1993) 17 Cal.App.4th 842, 17 Cal.App.4th 842, 854 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256848/in-re-marriage-of-dekker/)
  Known gap: This holding was made in a case in which the trial court had found that the working spouse was the primary reason for the business's growth, which pointed toward Pereira. Under the Van Camp approach, by contrast, the salary actually paid may be treated as the measure of the community's share (as in Van Camp itself and in Brooks, described elsewhere in this document); Dekker does not hold that a market salary is irrelevant, only that its payment does not by itself preclude apportionment. The dollar figure in the second quotation is specific to the Dekker record.

CASE LAW: BRANDES -- A HYBRID PEREIRA/VAN CAMP ALLOCATION IS PERMITTED, AND THE COMMUNITY'S INTEREST IS AN ALLOCATION, NOT OWNERSHIP
In In re Marriage of Brandes (2015), the Court of Appeal affirmed a trial court's use of a hybrid approach to a husband's investment-advisory business founded before marriage: Pereira for the early years of the marriage, when the husband's efforts were the primary reason for the business's growth, and Van Camp for the later years, when other factors were primarily responsible. The court held that the application of the hybrid approach achieved substantial justice between the parties and was not an abuse of discretion. Brandes also rejected the wife's contention that the community's Pereira share for the early period, not having been distributed, had become commingled with the business so that the community owned a percentage of the business itself. The court stated that it is well established that the community's interest in a spouse's separate business is confined to an equitable allocation based on the extent to which the spouse's personal efforts increased its value during the marriage, and that, absent commingling of separate and community funds, the community does not obtain an ownership interest in the business -- a rule the court concluded applies whether the trial court uses Pereira, Van Camp, or a hybrid of the two. The court further noted, following Patrick v. Alacer Corp. (2011), that the Moore/Marsden rule giving the community a pro tanto ownership interest in separate real property paid down with community funds does not apply to a spouse's expenditure of personal efforts on a separate business.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "It is well established that the community's interest in a spouse's separate business is confined to equitable allocation based on the extent to which the spouse's personal efforts resulted in increased value during the marriage."
  — In re Marriage of Brandes (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 1461, 239 Cal.App.4th 1461 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2902098/marr-of-brandes/)
  "We conclude that rule of law applies whether the court uses Pereira, Van Camp, or, as here, some hybrid thereof."
  — In re Marriage of Brandes (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 1461, 239 Cal.App.4th 1461 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2902098/marr-of-brandes/)
  "We are satisfied that the court's application of a hybrid Pereira/Van Camp approach achieves substantial justice between the parties."
  — In re Marriage of Brandes (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 1461, 239 Cal.App.4th 1461 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2902098/marr-of-brandes/)
  "Again, however, the Moore/Marsden rule is inapplicable to a spouse's expenditure of personal efforts on his or her separate business."
  — In re Marriage of Brandes (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 1461, 239 Cal.App.4th 1461 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2902098/marr-of-brandes/)
  Known gap: This is a single published Court of Appeal decision (Fourth Appellate District, Division One). The trial court's period-by-period findings on the causes of the business's growth were not challenged on appeal, so the hybrid approach was reviewed only for abuse of discretion on accepted facts. Brandes partially reversed the judgment on a separate issue (the lender's-intent doctrine as applied to shares purchased under a promissory note during marriage) not described here. The CourtListener text used for verification is the slip opinion as modified on September 9, 2015, which lacks Official Reports pagination; pin cites are therefore omitted for this decision. Brooks (2019), described in a later clause, cites Brandes at 239 Cal.App.4th 1473 for the "chief contributing factor" standard.

CASE LAW: SUBSTANTIAL GROWTH DURING MARRIAGE DOES NOT BY ITSELF CONVERT A SEPARATE BUSINESS INTO COMMUNITY PROPERTY
Brandes also rejected the argument that a separate-property business had become community property because it grew so dramatically during the marriage (in that case, from five employees to 514 and from $572,000 to $475 million in revenue) that it had become a different business. The Court of Appeal agreed with the trial court's determination that the business did not lose its separate property character by substantially growing in size and revenue during the marriage, distinguishing an earlier decision (Mueller v. Mueller (1956)) in which a business had been found to be community property because the owner failed to trace its original separate assets through commingling with community property. Brandes, quoting Patrick v. Alacer Corp., explained that California law accounts for community efforts devoted to separate property through equitable apportionment after the marriage, not through transmutation of the property during the marriage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "we agree with the court's determination that BIP did not lose its separate property character by substantially growing in size and revenue during the marriage."
  — In re Marriage of Brandes (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 1461, 239 Cal.App.4th 1461 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2902098/marr-of-brandes/)
  "Courts account for community efforts toward separate property through equitable apportionment after the marriage, not transmutation during the marriage."
  — In re Marriage of Brandes (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 1461, 239 Cal.App.4th 1461 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2902098/marr-of-brandes/)

CASE LAW: BROOKS -- APPLYING VAN CAMP WHERE THE SPOUSE'S EFFORTS WERE NOT THE CHIEF FACTOR, MEASURED BY COMPENSATION RECEIVED
In In re Marriage of Brooks (2019), the Court of Appeal affirmed a trial court's use of the Van Camp approach to apportion the appreciation during marriage of a husband's stock in an audio-technology company he had co-founded before marriage, where the evidence showed that his most significant contributions (the creation of the company's core products) had occurred before the marriage and that other factors were the chief cause of its growth afterward. The court explained that the legal criteria do not require a finding that the spouse made absolutely no contribution during the marriage before Van Camp may be applied; the question is whether the spouse's efforts during the marriage were the chief contributing factor causing the increase. Where Van Camp applies, the court next determines the reasonable value of the community's services and allocates that amount to the community. Brooks stated that under Van Camp the trial court considers the spouse's contribution by looking to his or her compensation during the marriage, and it upheld the finding that the husband's salary -- set from a recognized salary index and described by experts as competitive -- represented adequate compensation to the community, so that the remaining increase in the stock's value was his separate property.

CASE LAW: STANDARD OF APPELLATE REVIEW -- SUBSTANTIAL EVIDENCE FOR CHARACTERIZATION, ABUSE OF DISCRETION FOR THE CHOICE OF FORMULA
The decisions described in this document distinguish two questions on appeal. Whether a particular asset is separate or community property, and whether the facts call for equitable apportionment at all, are reviewed under the substantial evidence standard, meaning the appellate court asks only whether any substantial evidence supports the trial court's finding. The trial court's choice and application of an apportionment formula (Pereira, Van Camp, or a hybrid) is reviewed for abuse of discretion. Dekker stated both standards expressly, and Brandes reiterated that issues pertaining to the allocation of the community's interest in a spouse's separate business are reviewed for abuse of discretion, describing that standard as asking whether the trial court's ruling falls within the permissible range of options set by the legal criteria and placing the burden on the complaining party to establish a clear case of abuse.

As a general rule, property acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in California is community property, except as otherwise provided by statute. This baseline rule is one of the two statutory starting points for the apportionment question addressed by this document, because the earnings a spouse produces through personal skill, effort, and labor during the marriage fall within it.

expectedJSON.body: The Family Code provides that the separate property of a married person includes all property the person owned before marriage, all property acquired after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent, and the "rents, issues, and profits" of that property. A business owned before marriage is therefore separate property, and so, in general, is income the business produces on account of its own capital and character. Read together with the community property rule in the preceding clause, this provision creates the apportionment question the courts have addressed: when a separate-property business grows or produces profit during marriage partly because of its own capital and partly because of the owning spouse's personal effort (which is a community asset), some allocation between the two estates is required.

expectedJSON.body: In Pereira v. Pereira (1909), the California Supreme Court reviewed a divorce judgment that had treated all of a husband's business gains after marriage as community property, without any allowance for the $15,500 of separate capital he had invested in the business before marriage. The Court held this was error. It reasoned that the capital was the husband's separate estate; that although the principal part of the large income was clearly due to the husband's personal character, energy, ability, and capacity (a share that was "of course" community property), the business could not have been carried on without the capital; and that, absent circumstances showing a different result, some of the profits are presumed justly due to the capital invested. The Court directed that the probable contribution of the capital be determined from all the circumstances, and that for a profitable business it would amount at least to the usual interest on a long, well-secured investment. The apportionment method that developed from this decision -- allocating a fair return on the separate capital to the separate estate and the excess of the profits or growth to the community -- is commonly called the Pereira approach.

citations.case: Pereira v. Pereira (1909) 156 Cal. 1
citations.quote: This capital was undoubtedly his separate estate. The fund remained in the business after marriage and was used by him in carrying it on. The separate property should have been credited with some amount as profit on this capital. It was not a losing business but a very profitable one. It is true that it is very clearly shown that the principal part of the large income was due to the personal character, energy, ability, and capacity of the husband. This share of the earnings was, of course, community property. But without capital he could not have carried on the business.

citations.case: Pereira v. Pereira (1909) 156 Cal. 1
citations.quote: The probable contribution of the capital to the income should have been determined from all the circumstances of the case, and as the business was profitable it would amount at least to the usual interest on a long investment well secured.

The Court did not state a specific percentage as the fair return; it described only a floor ("at least" the usual interest on a long, well-secured investment) and left the amount to be determined on remand from all the circumstances. The decision does not use the label "Pereira approach"; that label was attached by later courts, as described in the Beam clause of this document. The Court also reversed the community property finding for retrial rather than fixing the apportionment itself.

expectedJSON.body: In Van Camp v. Van Camp (1921), the Court of Appeal considered a husband who owned, before marriage, most of the stock of a sea food packing corporation he had organized, who devoted his exclusive time and effort to managing it during the marriage, and who was paid a salary by the corporation for doing so. The wife argued, relying on Pereira, that the community should receive all profits above a seven percent return on the capital. The court found the Pereira circumstances inapplicable on those facts. It reasoned that, although the corporation's success was to a large extent due to the husband's capacity and ability, the business could not have been conducted without the invested capital, and the husband had been paid what the evidence showed was an adequate salary for services that another person of equal capacity could have been hired to perform. The court concluded that the husband's compensation must be deemed the extent of his personal earnings (community property), and that the balance of the business's profits was attributable to the capital invested (separate property), just as if he had not been employed by the corporation. The resulting method -- valuing the community's services, allocating that amount to the community, and treating the remainder as separate property -- is commonly called the Van Camp approach.

expectedJSON.body: The California Supreme Court in Beam v. Bank of America (1971) restated the principle underlying both approaches: because income arising from a spouse's skill, efforts, and industry is community property, the community is entitled to a fair share of the profits that derive from the spouse's devotion of more than minimal time and effort to handling his or her separate property. The Court of Appeal in In re Marriage of Dekker (1993) read Pereira the same way, stating that where more than minimal community effort combines with a separate capital investment to increase the value of the separate investment, the court must determine the amount of the increase attributable to the capital and the amount attributable to community effort. In In re Marriage of Brooks (2019), the Court of Appeal observed that the decision to apportion at all presupposes that the spouse made more than minimal contributions to the separate-property business during the marriage; if the contributions were minimal, no apportionment method would need to be chosen because there would be no potential community interest. Under these decisions, the threshold question is whether the spouse's efforts during marriage exceeded a minimal level; only then does the choice between the Pereira and Van Camp approaches arise.

expectedJSON.body: In Beam v. Bank of America (1971), the California Supreme Court described the two "quite distinct, alternative approaches" California courts had evolved for allocating earnings between separate and community income when a spouse devotes effort to separate property. The Pereira approach, the Court explained, is to allocate a fair return on the separate property investment as separate income and to allocate any excess to the community as arising from the spouse's efforts. The Van Camp approach is to determine the reasonable value of the spouse's services, allocate that amount as community property, and treat the balance as separate property attributable to the normal earnings of the separate estate. The two methods therefore start from opposite ends: Pereira fixes the separate estate's share first (a return on capital) and gives the community the remainder, while Van Camp fixes the community's share first (the value of the services) and gives the separate estate the remainder.

expectedJSON.body: Beam also stated the governing principle for choosing between the two approaches. Quoting earlier Court of Appeal authority, the California Supreme Court explained that California courts have developed no precise criterion or fixed standard for making the apportionment, but have endeavored to adopt the yardstick that is most appropriate and equitable in the particular situation, depending on whether the character of the capital investment in the separate property or the personal activity, ability, and capacity of the spouse is the chief contributing factor in producing the income and profits. In applying this principle, the trial court is not bound either to adopt a predetermined percentage as a fair return on separate business capital (the Pereira approach) nor to limit the community interest to a salary fixed as the reward for a spouse's services (the Van Camp method), but may select whichever formula will achieve substantial justice between the parties. Later decisions, including Dekker (1993), Brandes (2015), and Brooks (2019), have repeated this formulation as the controlling standard.

The trial court there had adopted the legal interest rate of seven percent simple interest as the reasonable rate of return on the husband's separate property. The wife argued on appeal that this figure was unrealistically high, but she had introduced no evidence at trial supporting any other, more realistic rate. The California Supreme Court, citing its earlier decision in Weinberg v. Weinberg (1967), stated that in the absence of such evidence the trial court correctly adopted the rate of legal interest. The court held that the application of the hybrid approach achieved substantial justice between the parties and was not an abuse of discretion. The court stated that it is well established that the community's interest in a spouse's separate business is confined to an equitable allocation based on the extent to which the spouse's personal efforts increased its value during the marriage, and that, absent commingling of separate and community funds, the community does not obtain an ownership interest in the business -- a rule the court concluded applies whether the trial court uses Pereira, Van Camp, or a hybrid of the two. Brooks (2019), described in a later clause, cites Brandes at 239 Cal.App.4th 1473 for the "chief contributing factor" standard.

expectedJSON.body: Brandes also rejected the argument that a separate-property business had become community property because it grew so dramatically during the marriage (in that case, from five employees to 514 and from $572,000 to $475 million in revenue) that it had become a different business. The Court of Appeal agreed with the trial court's determination that the business did not lose its separate property character by substantially growing in size and revenue during the marriage, distinguishing an earlier decision (Mueller v. Mueller (1956)) in which a business had been found to be community property because the owner failed to trace its original separate assets through commingling with community property. Brandes, quoting Patrick v. Alacer Corp., explained that California law accounts for community efforts devoted to separate property through equitable apportionment after the marriage, not through transmutation of the property during the marriage.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Brandes (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 1461
citations.quote: we agree with the court's determination that BIP did not lose its separate property character by substantially growing in size and revenue during the marriage.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Brandes (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 1461
citations.quote: Courts account for community efforts toward separate property through equitable apportionment after the marriage, not transmutation during the marriage.

expectedJSON.gap: The holding rests in part on the parties' stipulation of the business's value at the date of marriage, which relieved the owning spouse of any need to trace his original separate investment; Brandes expressly distinguished cases in which the community property presumption arose from commingling and the owner could not trace. This clause does not describe the law of commingling and tracing, or the circumstances in which a business acquired before marriage may be found to have been transmuted to community property by agreement, which are governed by other statutes and decisions not cited here. The second quotation is Brandes's quotation of Patrick v. Alacer Corp. (2011) 201 Cal.App.4th 1326, 1343-1344.

expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Brooks (2019), the Court of Appeal affirmed a trial court's use of the Van Camp approach to apportion the appreciation during marriage of a husband's stock in an audio-technology company he had co-founded before marriage, where the evidence showed that his most significant contributions (the creation of the company's core products) had occurred before the marriage and that other factors were the chief cause of its growth afterward. The court explained that the legal criteria do not require a finding that the spouse made absolutely no contribution during the marriage before Van Camp may be applied; the question is whether the spouse's efforts during the marriage were the chief contributing factor causing the increase. Where Van Camp applies, the court next determines the reasonable value of the community's services and allocates that amount to the community. Brooks stated that under Van Camp the trial court considers the spouse's contribution by looking to his or her compensation during the marriage, and it upheld the finding that the husband's salary -- set from a recognized salary index and described by experts as competitive -- represented adequate compensation to the community, so that the remaining increase in the stock's value was his separate property.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Brooks (2019) 33 Cal.App.5th 576
citations.quote: The relevant legal criteria do not require the trial court to find Husband made absolutely no contribution to the increase in value during the marriage in order to apply the Van Camp apportionment method.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Brooks (2019) 33 Cal.App.5th 576
citations.quote: The law is clear that under the Van Camp method, where a party's contributions are not the chief factor in the separate property business's growth during the marriage, the trial court still considers the spouse's contribution to the business by looking to his or her compensation during the marriage.

expectedJSON.gap: This is a single published Court of Appeal decision (Sixth Appellate District) applying a substantial-evidence standard of review to the trial court's factual findings and an abuse-of-discretion standard to its choice of formula; the court acknowledged that the trial court's finding of "no" contribution by the husband after marriage was likely overstated but affirmed on the ground that his contributions were not the chief factor. The CourtListener text carries the California Reporter (Cal.Rptr.3d) star pagination rather than Official Reports pagination, so Official Reports pin cites are omitted. The decision does not describe how the reasonable value of the community's services is measured when the working spouse received no salary or an inadequate one.

expectedJSON.body: The decisions described in this document distinguish two questions on appeal. Whether a particular asset is separate or community property, and whether the facts call for equitable apportionment at all, are reviewed under the substantial evidence standard, meaning the appellate court asks only whether any substantial evidence supports the trial court's finding. The trial court's choice and application of an apportionment formula (Pereira, Van Camp, or a hybrid) is reviewed for abuse of discretion. Dekker stated both standards expressly, and Brandes reiterated that issues pertaining to the allocation of the community's interest in a spouse's separate business are reviewed for abuse of discretion, describing that standard as asking whether the trial court's ruling falls within the permissible range of options set by the legal criteria and placing the burden on the complaining party to establish a clear case of abuse.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Dekker (1993) 17 Cal.App.4th 842
citations.quote: We apply the substantial evidence test to the judicial estoppel issue and to the issue whether equitable apportionment should be applied to this case. We apply the abuse of discretion test to the court's application of Pereira.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Brandes (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 1461
citations.quote: Issues pertaining to the allocation of the community's interest in a spouse's separate business are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

expectedJSON.gap: These standards of review describe how an appellate court examines a trial court's ruling; they are not themselves substantive rules of apportionment. Dekker's statement was made in rejecting an argument that the applicability of equitable apportionment was a pure question of law reviewable de novo. Brandes's formulation of the abuse-of-discretion standard quotes a decision outside the family law context (Hahn v. Diaz-Barba (2011) 194 Cal.App.4th 1177), which is not separately verified here.
